children: By Suzanne Vranica and Sarah Nassauer
To understand how Walmart obsesses over its customers, Seth Dallaire suggests picturing how K-pop fans study every move of the band BTS.

The retailer's chief growth officer is big on customer data and big on storytelling. The key to getting buy-in, Dallaire said, has been translating the unfamiliar ad-speak and strategies he picked up in jobs at tech companies, like monetizing shopper data, into the language his Walmart colleagues know: a relentless focus on lowering costs for customers.

"You really have to be part of the furniture," Dallaire said in an interview. "I'm going to sit in your meetings, I'm going to learn as much as I can...My ask back is just some reciprocity: that you be willing to listen to me."

Dallaire, 56 years old, spent most of his career building the advertising business at Amazon and was doing the same at Instacart when Walmart recruited him five years ago as a rare outside senior hire. Earlier this year Dallaire was promoted to oversee nearly all of Walmart's high-growth businesses globally.

Walmart executives have long touted the potential to monetize the data it collects on the 280 million people who pass through its nearly 11,000 stores and digital channels each week in 19 countries. They anonymize it and sell the insights into shopper behavior to product manufacturers that sell their wares through Walmart. Access to this consumer data has created a huge ad business.
Dallaire is under pressure to boost revenue and profits. Walmart's domestic in-store sales have slowed and rival Amazon unseated it as the largest U.S. company by annual revenue earlier this year.
Walmart generated nearly $6.4 billion in global ad revenue in its last fiscal year, a fraction of Amazon's $68.6 billion, according to the companies.
Raised in Seattle, Dallaire was captain of the lacrosse team at Vassar College and went on to earn an M.B.A. from New York University's Stern School of Business.

He envisioned a career in music or media, but changed course while sharing an office space with two employees of instant-messaging startup Mirabilis, during his summer internship at a micropayments startup. He watched them skateboard through the office — actually an apartment space on Manhattan's West 4th Street — high-fiving over their recent sale to AOL, a deal valued at roughly $400 million.

"It was super exciting," Dallaire said on a 2023 episode of "Grit," a podcast hosted by Kleiner Perkins partner Joubin Mirzadegan. "They were fired up and I'm like, 'Holy smokes.'" Dallaire was hooked on tech.

He started as an account manager in business development at Amazon but quickly turned to ads, taking roles at Microsoft and then Yahoo. More than a decade later, he returned to Amazon and helped build its fledgling ad operations into the third largest digital ad business in the U.S., behind Google and Meta Platforms, with about $10 billion in ad revenue by the time he departed, according to Emarketer.
Dallaire hosted team holiday parties at his parents' Seattle home in the early days. His mom and dad passed out hors d'oeuvres and mingled with the staff. He expensed pizza and beer kegs.
Instacart in 2019 recruited Dallaire, who had established a reputation for driving revenue by connecting shopper data, ads, e-commerce and ad measurement.
Walmart's ad business was slow to build, with false starts and resets before it convinced Dallaire to join in 2021.

As Walmart chief growth officer, Dallaire must win over clients accustomed to the advertising world's wine-and-dine courtships, while staying within Walmart's strict rules that it traces to founder Sam Walton's ethos of spending as little as possible to pass along lower prices to shoppers. Walmart executives are prohibited from offering or accepting even a free cup of coffee when doing business deals.

At the annual Cannes Lions ad festival in June, Walmart spent roughly $3 million, according to people familiar with the matter, to entertain clients with a DJ and Americana food including bite-sized burgers, fries and ice cream on a hotel roof and a suite to show off new ad offerings. Dallaire paid out of pocket for the drinks used to toast his birthday. Amazon, meanwhile, poured millions into an immersive, acre-sized space complete with espresso martinis, a fountain spouting rosé and caricature artists drawing portraits of attendees.
At Walmart, Dallaire found he had to overcome internal friction over giving priority to ad sales.

Store merchants historically negotiated directly with consumer brands for shelf placement, and when centralized ad teams tried selling digital banner ads online, merchants worried their trade budgets would disappear, former employees said.

After learning the term "cart rail," a prominent pallet of goods displayed at the store entrance — say, a stack of ketchup bottles during grilling season — Dallaire used the term to translate for store-focused colleagues that a home-page banner ad on the Walmart app is the digital equivalent. It creates awareness for shoppers entering a digital storefront.

Dallaire showed skeptics how ad profits can make their way back to merchant budgets, a lifeline for low-margin categories like food, and can be reinvested to lower prices or remodel stores. While physical retail operates on razor-thin operating margins, often 2% to 3% for grocery items, digital advertising can boast profit margins of 70% to 90%.

With Dallaire, "everything is backed by data," said Lisa Utzschneider, a veteran ad tech executive who worked with Dallaire at Amazon more than a decade ago. He is known for his methodical approach, sifting through numbers-heavy presentations and zeroing in on anomalies to pinpoint issues or identify new growth opportunities.

Dallaire embraced Bentonville, Ark., a company town where Sam Walton's heirs have funded a prestigious art museum, restaurants, cafes and a STEM school. He first commuted to the job from California, before building a home a few blocks off the central square where Walton opened a five-and-dime store in 1950.

Dallaire spearheaded Walmart's $2.3 billion Vizio acquisition in 2024, which catapulted the retailer into electronics manufacturing and into the streaming business via WatchFree+, Vizio's free, ad-supported streaming service. To explain to colleagues why Walmart should buy a TV brand in pursuit of shopper data and ad revenue, he often used the analogy of his grandparents' 1950s-style wooden TV console cabinet. Then, hardware was so important that a TV was considered stylish furniture. Now it's all about the software inside, he would say.

And earlier this year, Dallaire led Walmart's $1.4 billion purchase of Vibe.co, an ad tech platform that works with small and midsize businesses to expand Walmart's share of streaming TV ad spend. Smaller brands have been a key growth area for Meta and Amazon.

He now oversees Walmart's ad business, which sells in-store and digital ads, the Walmart+ subscription business, an online marketplace where third-party sellers list goods, and smart TV maker Vizio. Those businesses account for roughly one-third of the retail giant's total operating income.
Dallaire said he tries to balance Walmart's past with its quickly evolving future.

Walmart recently demolished its headquarters building, a low-slung and dingy former warehouse it used since 1971 that embodied the company's low-cost ethos, and moved into a sprawling new office complex. Dallaire stopped by to pick up a brick from the rubble as a keepsake.
"I've only been here five years," he said, but "I do have some nostalgia for it."
